checkpoints.answer: 2024-01-05, Alaska Airlines flight 1282, Boeing 737-9 N704AL, PDX to ONT, returned to PDX.

scheduled domestic passenger flight from PDX to Ontario, California (ONT)

checkpoints.answer: 1712:33 cabin pressure drop at ~14,830 ft; max 16,320 ft at 1713:41; landed 1726:46 (~14 min later).

evidence.quote: FDR data showed that, at 1712:33, the airplane was climbing through about 14,830 ft when the cabin pressure dropped
at 1713:41, the airplane reached its maximum altitude of 16,320 ft then began to descend
FDR data showed that the flight landed at 1726:46, about 14 minutes after the MED plug separated.

checkpoints.answer: 1 FA + 7 passengers minor; 2 pilots, 3 FAs, 164 passengers uninjured (177 occupants); 2 extra passengers sought observation without documented injuries.

checkpoints.answer: No bolt contact damage on 4 bolt holes; washer outlines; parallel dirt lines => incremental upward movement on prior flights.

evidence.quote: These lines were evidence that the left MED plug had moved incrementally upward during previous flight cycles.

the absence of bolt contact damage or deformation around the holes associated with the vertical movement arrestor bolts and upper guide track bolts indicates that the four bolts that should have been installed to prevent the left MED plug’s upward movement were missing before the plug moved upward off the stop pads.
Faint outlines associated with the upper guide track bolt washers were observed around the upper guide track bolt holes, indicating that hardware was installed at one time.

checkpoints.answer: Rivet rework; plug open by 1053 on 2023-09-18 until at least 1709 on 09-19; closed on second shift 09-19 with no door team on duty; no removal record so no QA; ~1839 photo.

evidence.quote: The investigation determined the left MED plug was open at least as early as 1053 on September 18, 2023, and remained open until at least 1709 on September 19, 2023
the left MED plug was closed during second shift operations that day, when no door team members were on duty.
texts included a photograph sent about 1839 that showed the plug in a closed position with no attachment hardware in the three locations visible
No removal record for opening the left MED plug was identified in CMES
Due to the absence of a removal record indicating that the left mid exit door plug installation had been disturbed, no quality assurance inspection of the plug closure was performed.

checkpoints.answer: Probable cause: Boeing failure to provide adequate training, guidance, oversight for parts removal process. Contributing: FAA ineffective compliance enforcement surveillance and audit planning.

evidence.quote: the probable cause of this accident was the in-flight separation of the left mid exit door (MED) plug due to Boeing Commercial Airplanes’ failure to provide adequate training, guidance, and oversight
Contributing to the accident was the Federal Aviation Administration’s ineffective compliance enforcement surveillance and audit planning activities

checkpoints.answer: BPI lacked clarity, >=10-yr compliance history; unstructured OJT; no change management for workforce experience.

evidence.quote: lacked clarity, conciseness, and ease of use necessary to be an effective tool
which had a documented history of compliance issues for at least 10 years before the accident.
on-the-job training was unstructured, undocumented, and focused primarily on routine build tasks
did not conduct a change management assessment to identify and address the risks associated with using a workforce with reduced experience
